title: The Condon Committee and the end of Blue Book, 1966-69
notes: Carries the Hippler letter of 16 January 1967 and the Bolender memo, which kept reports bearing on national security outside Blue Book.

lead.text: Six months after a one-day House hearing in April 1966, the Air Force contracted the University of Colorado to study UFOs under Edward U. Condon. The Air Force then cited the Colorado study and a National Academy of Sciences review of it when it ended Project Blue Book on 17 December 1969.

summary.text: The study followed public pressure: Gerald Ford, then House Minority Leader, called for hearings in late March 1966 after the Michigan sightings and the swamp gas explanation, and the House Armed Services Committee held its hearing on 5 April 1966.

The project was formed on 6 October 1966 under Air Force contract 44620-67-C-0035, with Condon as scientific director and Assistant Dean Robert J. Low of the Graduate School as coordinator, and it was released in January 1969.

Two sets of papers frame how it was set up: Low's internal memorandum of 9 August 1966, written before the project existed, and the letters exchanged in January 1967 between the project and Lt Col Robert R. Hippler of Air Force headquarters about what the Air Force wanted from it.

The study was the stated basis for closing Blue Book, and a memorandum by Brig. Gen. C. H. Bolender of 20 October 1969 recommending closure also said that reports bearing on national security went through other channels and were not part of the Blue Book system.

record.text: The report's title page and letter of transmittal place the work under Air Force contract 44620-67-C-0035 with the University of Colorado. The report's own account of its formation names Condon as scientific director, Low as project coordinator, and Stuart Cook and Franklin E. Roach as principal investigators.

The contract was let on 6 October 1966, six months after the House Armed Services hearing. A second congressional proceeding, the House Committee on Science and Astronautics symposium of 29 July 1968, heard J. Allen Hynek, James E. McDonald and Carl Sagan among others.

Low's memorandum of 9 August 1966, nearly two months before the project was formally established, says the study would be conducted almost entirely by nonbelievers, and that the trick would be to describe the project so that, "to the public, it would appear a totally objective study" while presenting to scientists the image of a group of nonbelievers.

Hippler wrote to Condon on 16 January 1967 that, once acquainted with the true state of affairs, the project must consider the cost of the Air Force UFO programme and whether the taxpayer should support it for the next decade. The letter adds that extending the contract, if needed, "would be less costly than another decade of operating Project Blue Book."

Low replied to Hippler on 27 January 1967, copying Condon, that on the second page Hippler had indicated what he believed the Air Force wanted of the project, and that he was very glad to have that opinion.

Section V Chapter 2 of the report records that staff members prepared a classified Estimate of the Situation in July 1948 asserting that UFOs were interplanetary, that Gen. Vandenberg rejected it for lacking proof, and that copies were destroyed.

In the same chapter, which Condon wrote, he praises the 1953 book by Donald H. Menzel, then director of the Harvard College Observatory, as excellent, noting that it is generally regarded as debunking and negative.

The report acknowledges McDonald's concurrent study as invaluable in bringing cases to its attention, records his 1967 trip to Australia, Tasmania and New Zealand to interview some 80 witnesses, and indexes him more heavily than any other outside critic. Its index also carries Low under the heading quoted on Fuller article.

The study drew reports from abroad: SEFAA, the Chilean aviation authority's service, records that the then director of its office, Coronel de Aviación Sergio Bravo Flores, circulated a request for reports to 43 aeronautical installations on 9 July 1968, and that part of what came back was sent to the Colorado commission.

Bolender, USAF Deputy Director of Development, signed his memorandum recommending termination on 20 October 1969. Secretary of the Air Force Robert C. Seamans Jr. announced the end of Blue Book on 17 December 1969, citing the Colorado study, the Academy review and prior Air Force experience.
Blue Book's records went permanently to the National Archives as 94 rolls of microfilm, T-1206.

claimed.text: John G. Fuller published the Low memorandum in Look in May 1968 as Flying Saucer Fiasco, calling the project a $500,000 trick. By Fuller's account, Condon then fired the investigators David Saunders and Norman Levine, who considered legal action alleging an unscientific approach.
The board records that the memo reached the press through McDonald, who received it from project staff and passed it on to Fuller.

McDonald publicly criticised the report on its release; the board records that he was ridiculed over his UFO work at 1971 congressional hearings on the SST and died by suicide in June 1971. It treats this as a documented sequence and asserts no cause.

On American Alchemy in 2024 and 2025, Jesse Michels and Robert Salas each described from memory an Air Force memo telling Condon that UFO research was a waste of money; neither produced it. The document that exists is Hippler's January 1967 letter.

Salas also said on the programme in July 2025 that he holds a handwritten note by Low recording that an Air Force colonel told him the Air Force blamed EMP from nuclear testing for the Malmstrom missile shutdowns and that the matter was probably too highly classified for the project. The note is not published and the board has not opened it.

Salas read on air what he presents as the project's record of an interview by Roy Craig with Lt Col Lewis D. Chase at Malmstrom on 19 October 1967, and says Chase had earlier confirmed in writing that he coordinated on the UFO activity before denying the connection to Craig.

Salas further said that J. Edgar Hoover wrote to Congress in 1949 identifying Condon as a Russian spy and that Lewis Branscomb urged Condon to take the Air Force study as a route back to a security clearance; he says twice that he does not know the details.

On the board's reading, Boulder is a template: the contracting agency obtained an academic verdict framed in advance, then used it to close its public reporting channel while national-security reports had never used that channel. The board likewise infers that the 1966 pressure produced a contracted study rather than an inquiry, and that neither the 1966 nor the 1968 proceeding produced any statute or continuing oversight.

The board also infers that the termination ended only the public-facing collection channel, leaving the Foreign Technology Division and AFOSI channels intact, and that no records series for the JANAP 146 side has ever been identified or accessioned.

contested.text: The Air Force's case for closing Blue Book was that no reported UFO was ever an indication of a threat to national security, that nothing showed technology beyond current knowledge, and that nothing showed unidentified sightings to be extraterrestrial vehicles. The Academy panel under Gerald M. Clemence found extraterrestrial visitation the least likely explanation and saw no case for a high priority.

The board's own caution on the Low memo is that it does not prove the report's conclusions were dictated, only that the coordinator planned to present the project differently to the public and to scientists before any data were examined.
Hippler's letter describes itself as informal, as his own opinion and as not binding on Condon, which is the strongest reading against treating it as an order.

The records disagree on who found the Low memo: one account has Saunders and Levine finding it in the project files, another has McDonald finding it there in July 1967, and a third has McDonald receiving it from project staff.
Air Force representatives and Rep. L. Mendel Rivers have asserted that no 1948 Estimate ever existed, against the report's own account of its preparation and destruction.

The board compares the report with Special Report No. 14 and infers that both summaries declared the subject unrewarding while leaving an unexplained residue, roughly a third of cases in the Colorado study. That figure rests on the board's inference, not on a cited count from the report.

Claims about Condon's past made on American Alchemy do not hold up against the record: Los Alamos credits the Primer lectures to Robert Serber and gives Condon the role of transcribing and compiling them into LA-1, and Michels's statement that Condon wrote the McMahon Act is uncited and not carried by the board.

questions: Why do the report's front-matter conclusions sit so uneasily with the unexplained residue in its own case chapters, and how many cases did the project itself leave unexplained?
Was the Low memo research design, or, as the university maintained, administrative caution about its reputation?
Who first found the Low memo in the project files, and how did it travel to Look?
Does the handwritten Low note that Salas describes exist, and what exactly does it record about Malmstrom?
What did Ford's March 1966 letters to the committee chairmen actually say?
What happened to reports made under JANAP 146 and AFM 55-11 after Blue Book closed?
